tier_reason: Well-known independent suite (alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks). report/data.js has mus (92/122 ns/op, 49 B), mus/unsafe_reuse (50/55 ns/op) and protobuf-go (287/356 ns/op, 51 B) rows from the same harness. The harness code is public, but the page and README give no CPU model or Go version (the report page says results are user-generated), so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: marshal 92 ns/op (50 ns/op mus/unsafe_reuse) vs protobuf-go 287 ns/op; unmarshal 122 ns/op (55 ns/op unsafe_reuse) vs 356 ns/op; total 214 ns/op (105 unsafe_reuse) vs 643 ns/op. Roughly 2.9-6.5x faster (marshal 3.1x/5.7x, unmarshal 2.9x/6.5x, total 3.0x/6.1x); wire size 49 vs 51 bytes (derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Shared report page (report/data.js, last regenerated 2025-07-04) states no CPU model or Go compiler version, so tier is capped at B. The mus rows are api_kind 'manual' (hand-written serializers built from mus-go primitives), while protobuf-go is codegen. The mus/unsafe_reuse numbers use unsafe string unmarshalling and marshal-buffer reuse.

notes: All numbers were confirmed against the raw data.js (a WebFetch summary misreported them; raw file checked via gh and raw.githubusercontent). The lower bound of the ratio range was 2.3x, which the page data does not support; corrected to 2.9-6.5x. last_commit on default branch main is 2026-05-07; 2026-05-27 was pushed_at from a non-default branch.

tier_reason: Well-known independent suite (eishay/jvm-serializers, about 3.3k stars) with public code, comparing protostuff with protobuf in the same run. The main wiki results give JVM 11.0.19 and only a generic '2.6 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i7' (no exact model, no JVM flags). The cited Staging-Results page gives no JVM or CPU at all, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Main jvm-serializers results (wiki Home, edited 2023-10-08, JVM 11.0.19): protostuff total (ser+deser) 1,261 ns vs protobuf 1,402 ns (~1.11x); ser 608 vs 875 ns (~1.44x); deser 653 vs 527 ns (protobuf ~1.24x faster); size 242 vs 242 bytes. Older Staging-Results page (last edited 2017-07-22): total 1,173 vs 1,950 ns (~1.66x), ser 444 vs 1,193 ns (~2.7x), deser 689 vs 689 ns (tie), size 239 vs 239 bytes (derived from page data)
corrections.workload: Serialize plus full deserialize of the 'media content' object tree (cycle-free, schema known in advance) in the eishay/jvm-serializers suite; times in ns per op; 'total' = ser + deser.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: JVM: Oracle Corporation 11.0.19 (wiki Home test platform); JVM flags not stated
corrections.hardware: 2.6 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i7 (exact model not stated), Mac OS X / Darwin Kernel 21.6.0, 12 logical cores (wiki Home)
corrections.caveats: Times are in nanoseconds, not microseconds (wiki Home: 'Ser Time+Deser Time (ns)'). 'total' is ser + deser and does not include create. The record's staging numbers come from a page last edited 2017-07-22 that states no JVM, flags, or CPU. The current main results (2023-10-08, JVM 11.0.19, generic Core i7, no JVM flags) show a much smaller total win (~1.11x), and there protobuf is faster at deserialization. The suite repo's last commit was 2023-10-07.

notes: Downgraded for an overstated/misstated claim, not for tier (stays B). The staging numbers are real but wrongly labelled µs, with 'total' wrongly described as including create, and they are superseded by the suite's current main results, which show ~1.11x total and ~1.44x serialize. benchmark_url repointed to the main wiki results. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 2,098 stars, last commit 2025-04-02, stale) all verified.

tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks Json table, updated 2026-07-19, shows 'D/ldc2 (Mir Asdf DOM)' at 0.133s vs 'C++/g++ (RapidJSON)' at 0.154s and 'C++/clang++ (RapidJSON)' at 0.194s. Code is public (json/test_mir_asdf.d uses dub package asdf ~>0.7.17 = libmir/asdf; json/test_rapid.cpp). Compilers are in the README, flags are in common/commands.mk and the dub.sdl header, and the CPU is an Intel Xeon E-2324G.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Mir Asdf (dub package asdf ~>0.7.17) built with D/ldc2 1.41.0 via DUB_BUILD = dub -q build --build=release-nobounds --compiler=ldc2 --single plus dub.sdl dflags -mcpu=native -linkonce-templates -enable-cross-module-inlining. RapidJSON built with g++ 16.1.0 (-std=c++23) and clang++ 22.1.8 (-std=c++23 -stdlib=libc++), COMMON_FLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (kostya/benchmarks common/commands.mk, json/Makefile, json/test_mir_asdf.d)
corrections.hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker base image Debian GNU/Linux forky/sid
corrections.workload: Parse a pretty-printed JSON file of 524,288 coordinate records (x/y/z floats, name string, nested opts object; json/generate_json.rb) and average x/y/z (kostya/benchmarks 'Json' test). Mir Asdf deserializes into typed structs (deserialize!Avg, ignoring name/opts), while RapidJSON parses into a full Document DOM. Both run in the same Docker image and on the same CPU.
corrections.caveats: Values are median ± median absolute deviation over repeated runs, not single runs. Margin vs default RapidJSON is ~1.16x (g++) and ~1.46x (clang++ with libc++). The page notes that default RapidJSON has number-parsing inaccuracies while the Mir-based D parsers are precise; against RapidJSON Precise (0.212s g++, 0.262s clang++) asdf is ~1.6-2.0x faster (derived from page data). Mir Asdf ties gason/yyjson (0.127-0.133s) and is ~2.2x slower than simdjson On-Demand (0.060s). This is one synthetic workload, and asdf's typed deserialization skips unused keys, while RapidJSON builds a full DOM.

notes: Numbers and tier A confirmed. The original compiler_and_flags wrongly attributed LDC2_BUILD -O5 to asdf; asdf actually uses DUB_BUILD release-nobounds with -mcpu=native. The original caveats wrongly said 'single-run' and '5-16%'. Metadata (BSL-1.0, 23 stars, last commit 2025-11-06, active) verified.
